bullets.text: ML is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI) focused on systems learning from data.
Models learn patterns from data to make decisions or predictions, rather than fixed rules.
Models improve over time with more data without needing reprogramming.
It's about teaching computers to learn from experience by providing data.
ML is ubiquitous: Netflix recommendations, spam filters, virtual assistants, facial recognition, fraud detection.
Popularity driven by access to huge amounts of data.
Increased computational power (GPUs) for data processing.
Development of sophisticated algorithms for extracting insights.
Most common type, trains models using labeled data (input + correct output).
Goal: learn input-output relationships to predict for new inputs.
Example: predicting house prices based on features and actual sale prices.
Categories: Regression (predicting continuous values like price) and Classification (predicting discrete labels like spam/not spam).
Uses unlabeled data; algorithms discover patterns, relationships, or structures independently.
Application: Clustering, grouping similar data points (e.g., customer segmentation).
Application: Dimensionality reduction, simplifying data with many features while preserving information.
An agent learns by interacting with an environment.
Receives feedback as rewards or penalties, adjusting its strategy.
Goal: learn a policy to maximize total reward through trial and error.
Examples: training robots, game-playing AI (AlphaGo), real-time decision-making in finance and self-driving cars.
Data quality: noisy, biased, or incomplete data degrades model performance.
Overfitting: model learns training data too well, failing to generalize to new data.
Ethical concerns: biased data can lead to biased models with serious real-world consequences.
ML requires understanding data, context, and the impact of models.
